lessons.title: Understanding Customs Brokerage in Africa
lessons.body: Customs brokerage is the professional service of preparing and submitting import and export documentation to clear goods through customs on behalf of a client. In Africa, this function is critical because cross-border trade is the lifeblood of many economies, yet customs procedures can be complex, opaque, and time-consuming. A customs broker acts as the intermediary between the trader and the customs authority, ensuring that all legal requirements are met while minimizing delays and costs. This lesson introduces the core concepts, the role of the broker, and the African trade landscape. Africa has 54 countries, each with its own customs laws, tariff schedules, and documentation requirements. However, regional economic communities such as ECOWAS, COMESA, SADC, and the East African Community have harmonized many procedures to facilitate trade. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is further reshaping the environment by reducing tariffs and simplifying rules of origin. A competent broker must understand both national and regional frameworks. The primary responsibilities of a customs broker include: classifying goods under the Harmonized System (HS) code, determining the correct customs value, calculating duties and taxes, preparing and lodging declarations, arranging for inspection, and advising clients on compliance. In many African countries, only licensed brokers can submit declarations electronically through systems like ASYCUDA, which is used in over 40 African nations. This means traders often cannot clear goods themselves without a broker. The business case for using a broker is strong. Mistakes in classification or valuation can lead to penalties, seizure of goods, or lengthy court battles. A broker reduces risk, speeds up clearance, and often saves money by applying preferential trade agreements correctly. For example, a trader importing textiles into Kenya from Egypt might qualify for reduced duties under the AfCFTA if the rules of origin are met. A broker who knows this can save the client thousands of dollars. To succeed in Africa, a customs broker must build relationships with customs officials, port authorities, shipping lines, and transport companies. They must also stay updated on frequent regulatory changes. This lesson sets the foundation for the rest of the module. In the following lessons, we will dive into classification, valuation, documentation, and special procedures. By the end, you will have a practical toolkit for operating as a customs broker in any African market.

lessons.title: HS Classification and Tariff Determination
lessons.body: The Harmonized System (HS) is an international nomenclature for classifying traded products. It is maintained by the World Customs Organization and used by more than 200 countries, including all African nations. Every product that crosses a border must be assigned an HS code, which determines the applicable tariff rate, any non-tariff measures, and eligibility for trade preferences. For a customs broker, correct classification is the single most important technical skill. An error can result in overpayment, underpayment, penalties, or even criminal charges. The HS code is a six-digit number at the international level, but most African countries extend it to eight or ten digits for national tariff lines. The first two digits identify the chapter, the next two the heading, and the next two the subheading. For example, 0901.21 refers to roasted coffee, not decaffeinated. A broker must use the General Interpretative Rules (GIR) to determine the correct code. GIR 1 says classification is determined by the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes. GIR 2 covers incomplete or unfinished articles. GIR 3 deals with goods that appear to fall under multiple headings, with the most specific description prevailing. GIR 4 covers goods that cannot be classified otherwise, using the heading for the most analogous goods. GIR 5 covers packing materials. GIR 6 ensures that classification at the subheading level follows the same rules. In Africa, many countries have national tariff schedules that add digits for statistical purposes or to apply specific duties. For instance, Nigeria uses the ECOWAS Common External Tariff (CET), which has five bands: 0 percent for essential social goods, 5 percent for raw materials, 10 percent for intermediate goods, 20 percent for final consumer goods, and 35 percent for specific goods for economic development. A broker must know these bands and how they apply. Practical steps for classification: First, obtain a detailed description of the product, including its composition, function, and packaging. Second, consult the HS Explanatory Notes and the Compendium of Classification Opinions. Third, use the GIR sequentially. Fourth, if uncertain, request a binding tariff ruling from the customs authority. Many African customs agencies offer advance rulings, which give legal certainty. Fifth, document your reasoning in case of audit. A common mistake is classifying by the product name rather than its essential character. For example, a smartphone with a camera is classified as a smartphone (8517.12), not as a camera (8525.80). Another mistake is ignoring chapter notes. Chapter 98 of many African tariffs covers special provisions for temporary importation or returned goods. A broker who misses this could pay unnecessary duties. To stay current, subscribe to WCO updates, attend national customs workshops, and use online databases like the AfCFTA tariff portal. Classification is not just a technical exercise; it is a commercial decision that affects landed cost. A broker who classifies accurately and defensibly adds real value to clients.

lessons.title: Customs Valuation and Duty Calculation
lessons.body: Customs valuation is the process of determining the value of imported goods for the purpose of calculating ad valorem duties and taxes. Most African countries follow the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement, which sets out six methods to be applied in hierarchical order. The primary method is transaction value, which is the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the importing country. If transaction value cannot be used, the broker must apply the other methods: transaction value of identical goods, transaction value of similar goods, deductive value, computed value, and fallback method. In practice, over 90 percent of imports are valued using transaction value. However, African customs authorities often challenge declared values if they suspect under-invoicing. This is a major risk area. A broker must ensure that the invoice price is supported by a contract, purchase order, proof of payment, and freight and insurance documents. Adjustments to transaction value include: commissions and brokerage (except buying commissions), cost of containers, packing costs, assists (materials, tools, etc. provided free or at reduced cost by the buyer), royalties and license fees related to the goods, and proceeds of resale accruing to the seller. Deductions are allowed for: freight and insurance after the place of importation, construction or assembly costs after importation, and duties and taxes of the importing country. In Africa, many countries use CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) as the basis for valuation, meaning the value includes transport and insurance up to the port of importation. Some countries like South Africa use FOB (Free on Board) plus a notional percentage for freight and insurance. A broker must know the specific rule for each country. Duty calculation involves applying the tariff rate to the customs value. For example, if a product has a 20 percent ad valorem duty and the CIF value is 10,000 USD, the duty is 2,000 USD. Additional taxes may apply: Value Added Tax (VAT), excise duty, environmental levy, and withholding tax. In Kenya, for instance, VAT on imports is 16 percent, calculated on the CIF value plus duty plus other taxes. In Nigeria, VAT is 7.5 percent. A broker must compute the total landed cost accurately. Practical tips: Always obtain a copy of the customs valuation database or reference prices used by the local customs office. These are often not public but can be accessed through experience. If you believe the customs value is wrong, you can appeal through a formal dispute resolution process. Many African countries have a customs appeal tribunal. Keep detailed records for at least five years, as audits can happen retroactively. Use a valuation worksheet that shows all adjustments. A common error is forgetting to include assists or royalties. Another is using the wrong exchange rate. Customs authorities publish monthly exchange rates; use the rate on the date of declaration, not the invoice date. For intra-African trade under AfCFTA, valuation rules are the same, but preferential tariff treatment requires a certificate of origin. A broker must verify that the origin criteria are met and that the certificate is valid. Valuation is the foundation of duty calculation. A broker who masters it can save clients money legally and avoid penalties. This lesson gives you the core knowledge to do that.

lessons.title: Documentation and Clearance Procedures
lessons.body: Documentation is the engine of customs clearance. Missing or incorrect documents are the most common cause of delays at African ports and borders. A customs broker must know the required documents for each country and each type of shipment. The core documents for imports are: commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading or airway bill, certificate of origin, import declaration form, and payment receipts for duties and taxes. For exports: commercial invoice, packing list, export declaration, certificate of origin, and any specific permits. In many African countries, additional documents are required. For example, in Nigeria, a Form M and a Pre-Arrival Assessment Report (PAAR) are mandatory for imports. In Kenya, an Import Declaration Form (IDF) and a Customs Declaration Form (CDF) are needed. In Ghana, a Customs Classification and Valuation Report (CCVR) is required. A broker must maintain a checklist for each country. The clearance process typically follows these steps: First, the trader provides the commercial documents to the broker. Second, the broker classifies the goods and determines the duty. Third, the broker submits the declaration electronically through the customs system (e.g., ASYCUDA, Kenya TradeNet, Nigeria Trade Hub). Fourth, customs may select the shipment for physical inspection or documentary check. Fifth, the broker pays duties and taxes. Sixth, customs releases the goods. Seventh, the broker arranges transport from the port to the final destination. Each step has potential bottlenecks. In many African ports, congestion and manual processes cause delays. A broker can mitigate this by pre-clearing documents, using electronic payment, and building relationships with customs officers and terminal operators. The role of the broker is not just to fill forms but to anticipate problems and solve them. For example, if a certificate of origin is missing, the broker can request a copy from the exporter or apply for a waiver. If customs questions the value, the broker can provide additional evidence. A key trend in Africa is the digitization of customs procedures. Many countries have implemented single window systems that allow traders to submit all documents through one portal. The ASYCUDA World system is used in over 40 African countries. A broker must be proficient in these systems. Another trend is the use of scanners and non-intrusive inspection, which speeds up clearance for compliant traders. Authorized Economic Operator (AEO) programs are also expanding. A broker whose clients are AEO-certified can enjoy faster clearance. Practical advice: Always verify the accuracy of the invoice and packing list against the actual goods. Discrepancies can lead to penalties. Ensure that the certificate of origin is properly stamped and signed by the authorized body. For AfCFTA, the origin declaration must follow the agreed format. Keep digital and physical copies of all documents. Use a document management system to track shipments. Train your clients on the importance of accurate documentation. Many delays are caused by clients providing incomplete or incorrect information. A broker who educates clients reduces their own workload. Finally, understand the customs law of each country. For example, in South Africa, the Customs and Excise Act sets out strict timelines for submission. In Egypt, the customs law requires pre-registration of importers. A broker must be a legal expert as well as a logistics expert. This lesson provides the framework; the next lesson covers special procedures and risk management.

lessons.title: Special Procedures, Compliance, and Risk Management
lessons.body: Beyond standard imports and exports, customs brokers in Africa must handle special procedures that offer duty relief or simplified clearance. These include temporary importation, transit, warehousing, free zones, and inward processing. Mastering these can create new business opportunities and save clients significant money. Temporary importation allows goods to enter a country without payment of duties, provided they are re-exported within a specified period. Common uses include equipment for construction projects, samples for trade fairs, and professional tools. In many African countries, a broker must obtain a temporary importation permit and post a security bond equal to the duties. If the goods are not re-exported, the bond is forfeited. Transit procedures allow goods to pass through one country to another without paying duties in the transit country. For example, goods from the port of Mombasa in Kenya destined for Uganda or Rwanda transit through Kenya. The broker must use a transit document, such as the COMESA Transit Document or the TIR Carnet, and ensure that the goods are sealed and tracked. Warehousing allows goods to be stored in a bonded warehouse without payment of duties until they are sold or removed. This is useful for traders who want to delay duty payment or re-export goods. Free zones, such as the Jebel Ali Free Zone in Dubai (not Africa) or the Lagos Free Trade Zone in Nigeria, offer duty-free treatment for goods that are re-exported or used in manufacturing for export. A broker must know the rules for each zone. Inward processing allows goods to be imported, processed, and re-exported with duty relief on the imported components. This is common in the textile and automotive sectors. Compliance is the bedrock of customs brokerage. Non-compliance can lead to penalties, seizure, and even imprisonment. The main compliance risks are: undervaluation, misclassification, false origin claims, and failure to declare. African customs authorities are increasingly using risk management systems to target high-risk shipments. A broker must implement internal controls to ensure accuracy. This includes: verifying client information, using a classification and valuation database, conducting periodic self-audits, and training staff. A key tool is the use of binding rulings. A broker can request an advance ruling on classification, valuation, or origin. This gives legal certainty and protects against penalties. Many African countries now offer advance rulings as part of their WTO commitments. Risk management also involves insurance. Customs brokers should carry professional indemnity insurance to protect against claims from clients for errors. In some countries, this is mandatory for licensing. Another risk is currency fluctuation. Duties are calculated in local currency, but invoices may be in USD or EUR. A broker must use the correct exchange rate and advise clients on hedging. Ethical conduct is essential. A broker must never facilitate smuggling, undervaluation, or corruption. While corruption exists in some African customs offices, a professional broker builds a reputation for integrity. This leads to faster clearance in the long run because customs officials trust the broker. Practical steps for special procedures: First, identify which procedure applies to the client's shipment. Second, gather the required documents, such as a bank guarantee or insurance certificate. Third, submit the application to customs before the goods arrive. Fourth, monitor the goods until the procedure is completed. Fifth, keep records for audit. For example, a broker handling a temporary importation of construction equipment into Ghana must ensure that the equipment is re-exported within 12 months. If the project is delayed, the broker must apply for an extension before the deadline. Failure to do so results in duty payment plus penalties. In conclusion, special procedures and compliance are where a broker moves from order-taker to trusted advisor. By mastering these areas, you can help clients navigate Africa's complex trade landscape, reduce costs, and avoid legal trouble. This lesson completes Module 2. In Module 3, we will cover advanced topics such as dispute resolution, digital tools, and business development.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Customs Brokerage Field Manual for African Agribusiness

Customs brokerage is not a paperwork exercise â it is a cash-flow and margin discipline. For African agribusinesses moving seed, feed, fertilizer, veterinary products, machinery, or processed food across borders, the difference between a broker who knows the tariff book and one who does not is measured in demurrage charges, spoilage, and lost contracts. This practical reference condenses the working knowledge a customs broker needs to clear agricultural consignments efficiently across African borders, with real figures and sources you can verify.

This lesson assumes you have completed the earlier modules on HS classification, valuation, and documentation. Here we focus on the operational reality: what to prepare before the truck arrives, what the numbers actually look like, and where the safety and compliance traps sit.

Why Agricultural Consignments Are Different

Agricultural goods are the most time-sensitive, documentation-heavy, and inspection-prone category of cargo in African trade. A container of day-old chicks cannot sit at a border post waiting for a valuation dispute to be resolved. A truck of fresh avocadoes crossing from Kenya to Tanzania has hours, not days, before quality collapses. A shipment of veterinary vaccines may require continuous cold-chain verification that customs officers are not equipped to assess.

This means the customs broker for agribusiness must operate as a pre-clearance specialist. The paperwork should be filed before the consignment reaches the border. The duty computation should be confirmed with the importer before the truck rolls. The inspection should be booked in advance. The broker who waits for the truck to arrive before starting work is already costing the client money.

Table 1: Typical Duty and Tax Burden on Selected Agricultural Imports (2024 estimates)

Note: Duty rates vary by country and by trade agreement (COMESA, SADC, ECOWAS, AfCFTA). Always verify against the current national tariff book and the applicable rules of origin. The figures above are indicative and drawn from published tariff schedules.

Table 2: Border Clearance Times and Costs for Agricultural Consignments (2023â2024)

Mombasa Port â Nairobi (Kenya) 72â96 150â300 per container Documentation & inspection Kenya Ports Authority, 2023

These figures illustrate a hard commercial reality: delays are expensive. A single day of demurrage on a container of perishables can exceed the broker's fee for the entire clearance. The broker's value proposition is speed and predictability, not just paperwork.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Veterinary Products, Pesticides, and Food Safety

Consignments containing veterinary medicines, pesticides, fumigants, or food additives must be handled under strict safety protocols. Many of these products are classified as hazardous under the WHO Recommended Classification of Pesticides by Hazard and the UN Globally Harmonized System (GHS). Customs brokers must verify:

  • Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) are present and match the declared product.
  • Transport and storage conditions comply with the manufacturer's label (e.g., MSD Animal Health, Aviagen cold-chain requirements).
  • Personal protective equipment (PPE) is available for anyone handling the consignment.
  • Expired or unregistered products are not cleared â they must be detained and reported to the national drug authority or veterinary services.

Failure to comply can result in public health incidents, legal liability, and permanent loss of broker licence.

Quick Reference Checklist for Agricultural Clearance

  1. Pre-arrival documentation package: Commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading/airway bill, certificate of origin, phytosanitary certificate, veterinary health certificate, import permit, and any product registration certificates.
  2. HS classification confirmation: Verify the 6-digit HS code and the national tariff line. Agricultural products often have multiple subheadings with different duty rates (e.g., seed vs. grain).
  3. Valuation check: Confirm the declared value against the transaction value, and be ready to justify with contracts, bank transfers, and price lists. Customs may challenge undervaluation.
  4. Duty and tax computation: Calculate import duty, VAT, excise (where applicable), IDF, RDL, and any levies. Confirm exemptions for agricultural inputs (seed, fertilizer, veterinary vaccines).
  5. Single Window submission: File through the national single window (e.g., Kenya TradeNet, Nigeria Trade Hub, Ghana ICUMS) before the consignment arrives.
  6. Inspection booking: Schedule phytosanitary, veterinary, or standards inspection in advance. For perishables, request priority inspection.
  7. Cold-chain and quarantine arrangements: Confirm that cold storage, quarantine pens, or fumigation facilities are available and booked.
  8. Post-clearance audit file: Retain all documents for at least 5 years. Customs audits can occur up to 5 years after clearance.

Further Reading and Official Resources

  • FAO â Trade and Food Safety: A Guide to the SPS Agreement (free PDF)
  • WTO â Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (official gateway)
  • African Union â AfCFTA Agreement and Protocols (free download)
  • World Customs Organization â HS Nomenclature 2022 Edition (official)
  • ILRI â Publications on Livestock Trade and Cross-Border Animal Health (free access)

Use this reference as a working tool. Keep it at the desk, update it with each national tariff change, and treat every agricultural consignment as a time-critical, compliance-critical operation. In African agribusiness customs brokerage, speed and accuracy are not optional â they are the product.

quiz.q: Which document is the primary declaration form used to clear goods entering the United States?
quiz.explanation: CBP Form 7501, the Entry Summary, is the core declaration used to provide classification, value, and duty information for imported goods.

quiz.q: What does HTSUS stand for in customs brokerage practice?
options: A) Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States
B) High Tariff Standard Union System
C) Hazardous Transport Safety Uniform Standard
D) Home Trade Security Uniform Schedule
quiz.explanation: HTSUS is the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States, which lists classification codes and duty rates for imported merchandise.

quiz.q: Which value method is generally used first when determining the customs value of imported goods?
quiz.explanation: Transaction value, based on the price actually paid or payable, is the primary and preferred method of appraisement.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a customs bond?
options: A) To insure cargo against damage
D) To guarantee payment of duties and compliance with customs laws
quiz.explanation: A customs bond guarantees that the importer will pay duties, taxes, and fees and comply with applicable customs regulations.

quiz.q: Which party is legally responsible for the accuracy of entry information submitted to CBP?
quiz.explanation: The importer of record is legally liable for the truth and accuracy of the entry data, even when a broker prepares the filing.

quiz.q: What does a customs broker use a Power of Attorney for?
options: A) To transfer ownership of goods
B) To act on behalf of an importer before CBP
C) To obtain a business license
quiz.explanation: A Power of Attorney authorizes a licensed customs broker to transact customs business on behalf of the importer.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a special tariff program that can reduce or eliminate duties?
quiz.explanation: The Generalized System of Preferences is a trade preference program that can provide duty-free treatment for eligible goods from designated countries.

quiz.q: What is the typical time frame for filing an entry summary after the entry is filed?
quiz.explanation: Entry summaries are generally required within 10 working days from the time of entry, unless an extension or alternative filing period applies.

quiz.q: Which body provides the harmonized system of tariff nomenclature used by most African customs authorities?
options: D) United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
quiz.explanation: The World Customs Organization administers the Harmonized System, which is the basis for tariff classification in most African countries.

quiz.q: In the HS, which level comes immediately after Section?
quiz.explanation: The HS hierarchy is Section, Chapter, Heading, Subheading, and national tariff lines.

quiz.q: A broker classifies imported solar panels under a heading that covers photovoltaic cells assembled in modules. This is an example of applying which classification rule?
quiz.explanation: GIR 1 uses the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes, which directly describe the goods.

quiz.q: Which document is normally used to declare goods and pay duties at an African port?
quiz.explanation: The customs declaration is the legal document by which the importer or broker declares goods and calculates duties.

quiz.q: Under the transaction value method, customs valuation is primarily based on which amount?
options: A) Retail price in the importing country
B) Price actually paid or payable for the goods
D) Domestic wholesale price in the exporting country
quiz.explanation: Transaction value is the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export, adjusted as required.

quiz.q: A consignment has a CIF value of USD 20,000 and the ad valorem duty rate is 25 percent. What is the duty payable?
quiz.explanation: Duty equals 20,000 multiplied by 0.25, which is USD 5,000.

quiz.q: Which of the following is added to the price actually paid or payable when determining customs value?
options: B) Cost of transport to the port of importation
D) Interest charges for deferred payment
quiz.explanation: Transport costs to the place of importation are generally added to transaction value under the CIF basis used in many African countries.

quiz.q: Why is correct HS classification important for an African customs broker?
options: A) It determines the applicable duty rate and trade measures
B) It replaces the need for a commercial invoice
C) It eliminates the need for customs valuation
quiz.explanation: Classification drives the tariff rate, preferential treatment eligibility, and regulatory controls.

quiz.q: Which valuation method is used when transaction value cannot be determined?
options: D) Transaction value of identical goods
quiz.explanation: The hierarchy moves to transaction value of identical goods before similar goods, deductive value, computed value, and fallback.

quiz.q: A broker notices the invoice price is unusually low compared to identical goods from the same exporter. What should the broker do?
options: A) Accept the invoice without question
B) Declare a higher value arbitrarily
C) Review for possible undervaluation and apply valuation adjustments
D) Ask the exporter to issue a new invoice with a higher price
quiz.explanation: Brokers must ensure declared value is accurate and may need to apply adjustments or query suspiciously low values.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes a customs broker in most African jurisdictions?
options: A) A government officer who assesses duty
B) A licensed agent who prepares declarations on behalf of importers
quiz.explanation: Customs brokers are licensed intermediaries who handle clearance documentation and compliance for importers and exporters.

quiz.q: Which document evidences the contract of carriage and serves as a receipt for goods?
quiz.explanation: The bill of lading is issued by the carrier and evidences receipt of goods and the contract of carriage.

quiz.q: A certificate of origin is most important for which purpose?
options: B) Claiming preferential tariff treatment under a trade agreement
C) Determining the weight of goods
D) Proving payment has been made
quiz.explanation: Certificates of origin support preferential duty claims under agreements such as AfCFTA or regional economic communities.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the AfCFTA for customs brokers?
options: A) To eliminate all customs documentation
B) To provide preferential tariff treatment among member states
C) To replace national customs authorities
D) To standardize currency across Africa
quiz.explanation: The African Continental Free Trade Area aims to reduce tariffs and trade barriers among member states, affecting classification and origin work.

quiz.q: A shipment arrives at the port but the importer has not paid duties. What is the likely customs action?
options: B) Storage of goods until duties are paid or secured
D) Return of goods to the exporter at no cost
quiz.explanation: Goods are generally not released until duties and taxes are paid or secured by guarantee.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a special customs procedure?
quiz.explanation: Temporary importation is a special procedure allowing goods to enter with conditional relief from duties.

quiz.q: What does risk management in customs clearance primarily aim to do?
options: B) Focus resources on high-risk consignments
quiz.explanation: Risk management allows customs to target high-risk shipments while facilitating low-risk trade.

quiz.q: A broker submits a declaration with an incorrect HS code, resulting in underpayment of duty. What is the most likely consequence?
options: A) No action because codes are optional
B) Penalties, duty adjustment, and possible investigation
C) Automatic refund of all duties
quiz.explanation: Incorrect classification can lead to penalties, recovery of short-paid duty, and compliance action.

quiz.q: Which Incoterm places the greatest responsibility on the seller for delivering goods to the buyer's country?
quiz.explanation: Delivered Duty Paid means the seller bears most costs and risks, including import duties, to the named destination.

quiz.q: A customs broker is calculating duty on goods with a customs value of USD 50,000, duty rate 10 percent, and VAT 15 percent on the duty-inclusive value. What is the total tax payable?
quiz.explanation: Duty is 5,000. VAT base is 55,000, so VAT is 8,250. Total tax is 5,000 plus 8,250, which equals 13,250. However, if the question asks for VAT only, the answer is 8,250.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key element of a post-clearance audit?
options: A) Reviewing past declarations and supporting documents
C) Reclassifying all goods at the border
quiz.explanation: Post-clearance audits verify compliance after release by examining records and declarations.

quiz.q: Why might a broker use a customs bond or guarantee?
options: A) To avoid all duties permanently
B) To secure duty payment and obtain release of goods before final assessment
C) To replace the bill of lading
quiz.explanation: Bonds and guarantees allow release while ensuring the government can collect duties if needed.
